                                  13          Before the Court are two administrative motions:
                                  14          (1) Point Financial, Inc.’s (“PFI”) Administrative Motion to Consider Whether PFI’s
                                  15              Response to Google LLC’s (“Google”) Emergency Motion to Enforce the Preliminary
                                  16              Injunction and for Contempt Sanctions Should be Sealed. ECF No. 151.
                                  17          (2) Google’s Administrative Motion to Consider Whether PFI’s Material Should be
                                  18              Sealed. ECF No. 156.
                                  19   For the reasons that follow, the administrative motion at ECF No. 151 is GRANTED as narrowed
                                  20   by Google, and the administrative motion at ECF No. 156 is GRANTED to the extent redactions
                                  21   are requested by Google.
                                  22     I.   LEGAL STANDARD
                                  23          “Historically, courts have recognized a ‘general right to inspect and copy public records
                                  24   and documents, including judicial records and documents.’” Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of
                                  25   Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (quoting Nixon v. Warner Commc’ns, Inc., 435
                                  26   U.S. 589, 597 & n.7 (1978)). Accordingly, when considering a sealing request, “a ‘strong
                                  27   presumption in favor of access’ is the starting point.” Id. (quoting Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto.
                                  28   Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1135 (9th Cir. 2003)). Parties seeking to seal judicial records relating to
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF            Document 170          Filed 02/09/26      Page 2 of 6




                                   1   motions that are “more than tangentially related to the underlying cause of action” bear the burden

                                   2   of overcoming the presumption with “compelling reasons” that outweigh the general history of

                                   3   access and the public policies favoring disclosure. Ctr. for Auto Safety v. Chrysler Grp., 809 F.3d

                                   4   1092, 1099–101 (9th Cir. 2016); Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178–80.

                                   5           In addition, in this district, all parties requesting sealing must comply with Civil Local

                                   6   Rule 79-5. That rule requires, inter alia, the moving party to provide “the reasons for keeping a

                                   7   document under seal, including an explanation of: (i) the legitimate private or public interests that

                                   8   warrant sealing; (ii) the injury that will result if sealing is denied; and (iii) why a less restrictive

                                   9   alternative to sealing is not sufficient.” Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(1). Civil Local Rule 79-5 requires the

                                  10   moving party to provide “evidentiary support from declarations where necessary.” Civil L.R. 79-

                                  11   5(c)(2). And the proposed order must be “narrowly tailored to seal only the sealable material.”

                                  12   Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(3).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           Further, when a party seeks to seal a document because it has been designated as

                                  14   confidential by another party, the filing party must file an Administrative Motion to Consider

                                  15   Whether Another Party’s Material Should be Sealed. Civil L.R. 79-5(f). In that case, the filing

                                  16   party need not satisfy the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(1). Instead, the

                                  17   party who designated the material as confidential must, within seven days of the motion’s filing,

                                  18   file a statement and/or declaration that meets the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-

                                  19   5(f)(3). A designating party’s failure to file a statement or declaration may result in the unsealing

                                  20   of the provisionally sealed document without further notice to the designating party. Id. Any

                                  21   party can file a response to that declaration within four days. Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(4).

                                  22    II.    ECF NO. 151
                                  23           PFI has filed an administrative motion to consider whether PFI’s Response to Google’s

                                  24   Emergency Motion to Enforce the Preliminary Injunction and for Contempt Sanctions should be

                                  25   sealed. ECF No. 151. Google filed a statement in support of sealing, which requests narrower

                                  26   redactions than those identified by PFI. ECF No. 153. PFI does not oppose Google’s request.

                                  27           Google requests to seal material pertaining to the “identity of one of the Vendors that

                                  28   manufacture, test, and assemble the chip at issue in this litigation.” ECF No. 153 at 3. Google
                                                                                            2
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF           Document 170         Filed 02/09/26     Page 3 of 6




                                   1   argues that the public disclosure of the identity of this vendor would give Google’s competitors

                                   2   and potential contracting partners unfair leverage in the marketplace. Id.

                                   3          As the sealing request relates to a response to a motion to enforce the preliminary

                                   4   injunction and for contempt sanctions, which the Court finds is “more than tangentially related to

                                   5   the underlying cause[s] of action,” the Court will apply the “compelling reasons” standard. Ctr.

                                   6   for Auto Safety, 809 F.3d at 1099–101. The Court finds that compelling reasons exist to seal the

                                   7   materials Google identifies, because the “compelling reasons” standard is met for confidential

                                   8   business information that would harm a party’s competitive standing if publicly disclosed. See

                                   9   Music Grp. Macao Com. Offshore Ltd. v. Foote, No. 14-cv-03078, 2015 WL 3993147, at *6

                                  10   (N.D. Cal. June 30, 2015); Jam Cellars, Inc. v. Wine Grp. LLC, No. 19-cv-01878, 2020 WL

                                  11   5576346, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 17, 2020) (finding compelling reasons for sealing “confidential

                                  12   business and proprietary information”); Fed. Trade Comm’n v. Qualcomm Inc., No. 17-cv-00220,

                                  17   competitive standing”). The Court also finds that the request is narrowly tailored. See Civil L.R.

                                  18   79-5(c)(3).
